lessons.title: Chain arithmetic: why 3 + 2 × 4 = 20
lessons.intro: Type 3 + 2 × 4 into this calculator and you get 20 — not the 11 you learned in algebra class. Out of the box the calculator works in chain order: it applies each operation the moment you press the next one, strictly left to right. This lesson shows that order in action, then uses parentheses to take back control.

steps.explain: Press CE/C twice to abandon anything already in progress, so we start clean at 0.00. This is a good habit at the top of any fresh calculation.
Key 3 and press +. The display settles to 3.00 — once a number is locked in, it is shown with two decimal places, the standard display format.

Key 2, then press ×. Watch closely: the display reads 5.00. The calculator finished 3 + 2 the instant you pressed the next operation key. That is chain order — multiplication gets no special priority.
Key 4 and press = to finish: 5 × 4 = 20. A calculator using algebraic rules would have answered 11 (2 × 4 first, then + 3) — same keys, different order.
Now force a grouping of your own. Key 7 and press × to begin 7 times something.
Open a parenthesis, key 3 + 5, and close it. The display shows 8.00 — the value of the part inside the parentheses. Parentheses make the calculator finish that piece before anything else.
Press = to complete the outer multiplication: 7 × 8 = 56.

lessons.answer: 3 + 2 × 4 = 20.00 in chain order, and 7 × (3 + 5) = 56.00. The calculator works left to right as you press keys — reach for parentheses whenever a piece must be computed first.

lessons.title: The % key: sales tax and a discount
lessons.intro: A $498 bicycle carries 7% sales tax, and a $69.99 sweater is marked 10% off. The % key handles both — you never convert a percentage to a decimal by hand. Its meaning depends on the operation key pressed just before it.

steps.explain: Clear any calculation in progress so the display reads 0.00.
Key the price, press +, key 7, and press %. Before you touch =, the display already shows 34.86 — the tax itself, 7% of 498. After + or −, the % key means "this percent of the first number".
Press = to add the tax onto the price: the bicycle costs 532.86 out the door.
Now the discount. Key 69.99, press −, key 10, and press %. The display shows 7.00 — the discount amount. (Inside, the value is 6.999; the screen rounds it to two places.)
Press = to take the discount off: the sweater's sale price is 62.99.
After × the % key behaves differently: it simply divides the number by 100. So 453 × 4 % = computes 453 × 0.04 — four percent of 453 is 18.12.

lessons.answer: $498 + 7% tax = $532.86, and $69.99 − 10% = $62.99. After + or −, % gives that percentage of the first number; after × or ÷, it just divides by 100.

lessons.title: Fixing typos: backspace vs CE/C
lessons.intro: Halfway through multiplying 1,234.56 by 3, your finger slips: the screen reads 1,234.86. The keypad has two erasers. The backspace arrow removes one character at a time and leaves the rest of the calculation standing, while CE/C abandons everything you had going. Knowing which to reach for saves you from starting over.

steps.explain: Start clean at 0.00.
Begin the calculation: key 3 and press ×.
Key the wrong number. While you are still typing, the display echoes exactly what you press (plus a comma grouping the thousands) — the two-decimal format only takes over once the number is finished.
Press the backspace arrow twice. Each press erases the rightmost character — first the 6, then the 8 — leaving 1,234. with a bare decimal point. The pending 3 × is untouched.
Type the correct ending. The number now reads 1,234.56.
Press = : 3 × 1,234.56 = 3,703.68. The typo never forced you to restart.
Now see what CE/C does instead. Start a new calculation: 5 × 27.
Press CE/C. The display returns to 0.00 — but it did more than erase the 27. Once an operation key like × has been pressed, CE/C abandons the whole calculation, not just the number.
Proof: key 9 and press =. You get 9.00, not 45.00 — the pending 5 × is gone.

lessons.answer: 3 × 1,234.56 = 3,703.68 after repairing the typo in place. Backspace edits the number you are typing and keeps the calculation alive; CE/C bails out of the calculation entirely.

lessons.title: The +/- key: entering negative numbers
lessons.intro: You are $4,500 in debt and pay off $1,000 — where do you stand? Financial calculators show money you owe or pay out as a negative number, and the +/- key is how you flip the sign. You cannot type a minus sign directly: the − key always means subtraction.

steps.explain: Start clean at 0.00.
Key the size of the debt.
Press +/- to make it negative — money owed. The key flips the sign of whatever the display is showing.
Add the $1,000 payment: −4,500 + 1,000 = −3,500. The answer stays negative because you are still in debt.
+/- works on a finished result too: one press flips −3,500.00 to 3,500.00. Press it whenever a value on screen has the wrong sign.

lessons.answer: −4,500 + 1,000 = −3,500.00 — still $3,500 in debt. Money going out is negative on this calculator, and +/- (never the − key) is how you set that sign. Remember this convention: it matters everywhere money changes hands.

lessons.title: One-press math: x², √x and 1/x
lessons.intro: Three keys act instantly on whatever number is showing — no = needed. x² squares it, √x takes the square root, and 1/x turns it into a reciprocal. We will square 6.3, take the root of 15.5, and invert 3.2.

steps.explain: Start clean at 0.00.
Key 6.3 and press x². The answer appears immediately: 6.3 × 6.3 = 39.69. No = required.
Key 15.5 — typing a new number simply replaces the old result — and press √x. The square root appears at once: 3.94 on screen (the exact value 3.9370... is rounded to two places).
Key 3.2 and press 1/x to compute 1 ÷ 3.2. The display shows 0.31 (exactly 0.3125 inside — the screen rounds, the calculator remembers the full value).

lessons.answer: 6.3² = 39.69, √15.5 ≈ 3.94, and 1/3.2 ≈ 0.31. These keys transform the displayed number the instant you press them — no = needed.
